rules.rule: A verification claim must run the real mechanism; a stub, mock, re-run test suite, health check or signature inspection standing in for it is a workaround — and the motive (stuck vs merely easier) does not change that.
Any implementation that routes around the real problem — case-by-case special cases, an extra wrapper to avoid a root cause — is the same failure as a fake verification: stop, disclose, fix.

Read-back must come from the truth owner. A UI render, a cache, an application log, console output, or the response body of the write itself is not authoritative proof; neither is a screenshot or an operator's prose. The proof environment must be the real provider or a pre-registered equivalent, never self-declared at proof time.
A claim about how an external system behaves is settled by one read-only observation of that system recorded verbatim — not by vendor docs, a code default, or a config file.
External writes leave an audit trail: actor, timestamp, trace id.

rules.rule: Reference versus clone: what may be consulted, what may be copied, and what may only be learned from.
Complex core logic is extractable from framework surfaces.
Config and runtime settings own no business rules, orchestration or hidden application logic.
Domain vocabulary is not polluted by transport or adapter naming, and the domain renders no transport output.
Projection failure must not alter truth-owning state, and a sync failure must not contaminate the truth workflow.
Ops and runtime assets are replaceable without touching core, and must not have become workflow truth.
Parsing that only shapes transport stays at the entry surface; parsing whose result drives a workflow or approval decision belongs to orchestration.
Multi-step operations stay atomic, or document the compensating action.
Objects returned to a pool or cache are clean; reset or invalidation happens at the right boundary.
Substitute detection by eye: self-defined schema fields replacing framework templates, and a harness that runs the orchestration shell while swapping out the mechanism actually at risk.
A cited mechanism must actually execute — an import, a comment, a string, a dead helper or an unexecuted branch is not proof.
The effective value comes from the resolver that runs, not from a config file plus a code default.
Artifact lifecycle: stable identity, collision prevention, cleanup, rollback, orphan handling.
Generated assets handle all five paths: persist, regenerate, blocked, moderation, failure.
Fan-out and batch work: bounded, per-item identity, partial failure, retry exhaustion.
Approval and manual-review flows: durable approval states, blocked and regenerate paths, operator proof.
Mock-only proof cannot cover persistence, integration or read-back obligations; mock evidence covers typed failure paths, not success or read-back.

Request fit: did the change actually deliver what was asked, without quietly narrowing scope or substituting a different requirement — and can request, implementation, proof and doc updates each be traced to each other?
A workflow, decision-flow or routing change produces a diagram, and the diagram marks truth owner, external write boundaries, forbidden paths, and at least one error path.
Shotgun surgery: the same rule or logic spread across three or more files needing lockstep edits.
Artifact entropy: runtime outputs, evidence, review logs and snapshots accumulating with no retention, archive or active-window rule, and staging artifacts left in the active reasoning path.
Semantic entropy: one concept carrying several names, one name covering several concepts, or retired terminology reappearing in new code.
The same code may be reported by two review axes only when the impacts differ and each impact is independently concrete.
Human-authored free-text values (form fields, config edits, spreadsheet cells) are untrusted regardless of source and are parsed before use.
A hardcoded list that must track reality will go stale; judge by property, or read from verified config. One missing entry means the rule silently stops applying.
Hunk-level scope: is this hunk necessary to complete the approved outcome?
Opportunistic rewriting disguised as feature delivery, or an unrelated rewrite carried in under a clean-replacement banner.
Legacy design patterns, abstractions or control-plane conventions imported into new code for convenience.
An approval gate present in the approved design must be enforced in the implementation.

Seven ownership slots are explicit: workflow truth, approval truth, file/media truth, which surfaces are projections, which are transport, which runtime metadata must never become product truth, and which derived surfaces must never write back to authority state.
Is the model a semantic selector or a tool caller, and who owns final validation, sequencing and side effects?
Each selectable action carries a usable purpose, when-to-use, when-not-to-use, schema, side-effect level, approval semantics and scope assumptions — and the negative guidance is actually informative.
Agent guardrails: transport never owns truth, advisory paths never mutate truth, the active action subset is mandatory, and a canonical preview precedes schedule mutation.
A newly required setting must reach the deployment command or manifest.
Where a fallback is provided for an unavailable config service, is the fallback value itself safe — does losing the value open or close?
Can you say, from the diff, which entry a secret arrived through?
Was runtime-fetched or platform-managed secret retrieval available, or was environment injection genuinely required here?
Background and worker paths can answer: did it start, did it run twice, which step failed, and did checkpoint, retry and cleanup behave as intended.
Logs distinguish provider failure from local failure.
Trace context is injected by middleware, not added by hand in each handler.
Hot paths use exact queries with a workable index strategy and do not over-fetch.
Lock contention and retry amplification are bounded — nothing slow inside a critical section.
Batch paths define memory caps, control disk pressure, and clean up temporary output.
Projection paths define a staleness tolerance and monitor reconciliation lag and quota pressure.
Scheduled and unattended work prevents overlap and duplicate execution.
Unattended workers bound artifact and log retention and monitor cadence drift.
Cold start cost is controlled and connection management prevents a connection storm.

Core paths are measured (at least p50), and the metric set matches the workload class — tail latency for interactive, throughput under bounded concurrency for batch, lag for async, quota for external, before/after for material changes.
Event-level sync loops: does A writing trigger B, which triggers A?
Auth is applied through unified wrappers rather than re-implemented per route.
Each service has its own identity with fine-grained permissions rather than sharing a broad credential.
Every reachable decision branch introduced by the change has a test, and loop boundaries cover zero, one and many.

Test generation considers all eight scenario classes: happy path, validation failure, authorization failure, dependency failure, retry/duplicate/replay, state transition, cleanup/rollback, and empty/boundary/malformed input.
Per-layer test focus and mock rule for each of the seven layers (config, domain, orchestration, execution units, adapters, projections, entry surfaces).
Long-lived processes are tested beyond the happy path: claim/lock, cleanup and artifact lifecycle, state transitions asserted on real state, checkpoint recovery, concurrency guard, failure handling.
Adapter tests cover request payload shape, response mapping, and error interpretation with retry.
Config tests cover missing required config crashing at startup, invalid format producing a clear error, and coercion.
UI components are tested across props, loading, empty and error states.
When a new test is genuinely stronger and covers the same invariant, the old one is deleted in the same commit.
Integration tests are few and aimed at the high-risk seams; external systems get contract tests or stubs.
A thread-through that changes a signature also enumerates callers and justifies the ones not threaded, so no dead caller path goes untested.
Where partial loading is expected, the expected endpoint is called, a full route reload is absent or within threshold, and status codes are as expected.
When a surface signal and the server response disagree, the server response is the root-cause truth — assertions must bind to it, not to the surface.
Console noise: a small allowlist for known non-blocking errors, new uncategorised errors surfaced, and no automatic failure on noise alone unless acceptance criteria are violated.

Runtime coverage questions per path type: request/response (did it arrive, where did it fail, why slow), background (did it start, did it duplicate, which step), stateful (which truth owner changed, where is the evidence), external (provider or local failure).
State invariants are implemented and transitions have explicit boundaries.
Heavy paths have isolation or batching guardrails, and connection, retry and lock behaviour is reasonable.
"Ran without error" is not proof: a zero-output command, an empty scanner stdout, or an unsupported check reporting completion all prove nothing.
Naming an obligation id does not cover it — restate the target, expected result, truth owner and read-back target, give an observed result, and point at a concrete observation.
Vague obligations such as "run the relevant tests" are invalid.
Declare the expected result before the run, never after seeing the output.
A one-off runtime or surface observation does not substitute for a committed test.
Two independently green branches do not make a green merge; the merged head is unproven until proved again.
Never edit the expectation to match the result.
A run blocked before its first real step, or that failed its own validation, is neither a pass nor a baseline candidate — and a baseline is never promoted automatically or overwritten without review.
Inapplicable items and no-change outcomes are written down with a reason; omission and inapplicability are indistinguishable on disk.
A quantified claim obliges enumeration: list the set, classify every member as covered or exempt, and mark exemptions inline. One grep is not an enumeration of a multi-hop chain.
A check whose scope was incomplete for any reason that could hide a finding is not green; report the range actually covered rather than reading partial as clean.
"Nothing to report" is a legitimate result; do not manufacture findings to show work.
A missing governance document does not remove the obligation: perform the step with built-in rules and state what was missing.
Read specs and contracts line by line and read a whole section before judging a fragment; do not skim or summarise.
Every document read must be used; never read one and then proceed on the original plan.
Scope is judged by the approved outcome, not by the number of files touched.
No unrelated cleanup, opportunistic redesign, speculative hardening, or rewrite carried in under a clean-replacement banner without explicit approval.
A problem found outside approved scope is reported and left alone until directed.
Being small is not a reason to skip source-of-truth, scope, proof or review.
Do not hide scope in commit messages or summaries.
The documentation a change requires belongs to that change, not to later cleanup — and a change labelled cleanup must not alter behaviour.
Grep returning nothing, and you not understanding something, are facts about your search and your reading — not about the thing. Neither is a reason to remove.
A guard that has never fired may have been internalised rather than made obsolete, and a young file has too short an observation window to judge. Neither is evidence of uselessness.
Before deleting anything unregenerable, confirm a copy exists in version control or elsewhere.
Archiving is deleting and relying on version control; do not create a directory to hold what you were afraid to delete.
Identical wording, identical structure, or the same topic does not make two things the same contract. A contract has one owner; a second copy is the next drift.
A rule violated long-term with nobody enforcing it must be either enforced or changed; leaving both undone is not an option.
Treating the symptom is not fixing, and the same class of failure appearing a second time means the first fix was in the wrong place.
Fixing an instance of a fault with another instance of the same fault class is not a fix.
Repair a finding everywhere the fact appears, not only where it was reported.
After a repair has failed twice, do not replay it: state the repeated root cause and a concrete difference before trying again.
Every retry records what was changed, the root cause, and what was learned. "Retried N times" is not a record.
When verification is structurally unreachable: revise the claim first, then narrow scope and record the carry-forward, and escalate only third.
Retry a transient failure once; never continue silently past a critical failure.
Do not report a failure mode you cannot point to as having actually happened, with evidence; scale risks the project's context does not support need a concrete failure mode first.
Do not require abstraction because a rule, acronym or preference says so; direct code is acceptable when the behaviour is simple, local and unlikely to diverge.
One finding per issue; do not merge unrelated issues because they share a theme.
Another agent's conclusion is not a fact — verify at least one of its claims yourself before acting on it.
Verify what was marked clean as well as what was flagged; the unflagged range is the blind spot.
Document precedence: architecture and current-state documents, then stack authority docs, then project instructions, then support guidelines, then references and cookbooks.
References, comparisons and cookbooks are informational input, not protected contracts or implementation templates.
An old system's or a donor repo's document is not evidence of current state; resolve against the current authority first.
Update the existing document by default; never add a parallel authority document for convenience or tidiness.
Never keep a second prose copy of an executable schema.

Start from the truth owner, not from the request surface: identify truth-owning layers, then orchestration and policy ownership, then read/write separation, then execution units, projections, entry surfaces and adapters.
Build order: contracts first, then pure logic, then adapters, then entry surfaces last.
When responsibility and name disagree, follow responsibility.
When principles collide: type safety, then separation, then extractability, then naming.
Converge legacy at the high-risk areas first — auth and permission, billing and credits, webhooks and external side effects, truth-owning state transitions. Do not rewrite everything you touch.
Optimising must not break correctness, truth, safety or idempotency; and choose the focus by workload class, not by deployment platform.
Declare "good enough" before optimising, and treat a performance claim without measurement as incomplete.
What must hold is the property, not the product: no vendor, cloud or tool becomes the requirement.
If changing a value requires changing behaviour or passing a new test, it is code, not config.
A targeted obligation must not become blanket; blanket is the failure it exists to prevent.
Stricter custom obligations are allowed; replacing or shadowing a standing obligation is not.
Deciding not to take a risk does not delete its proof obligation; the decision itself needs durable evidence.
Prose cannot cancel a derived obligation: name replacement lanes of equal strength, or record a typed reason with a real explanation.
Proof requirements are on by default; turning one off is a written, one-time project decision, not a per-task re-evaluation.
"The tool ran" and "the gate passed" are separate namespaces and must never be merged — the same applies to a review job completing versus a review passing.
Advisory scanner output is not a gate result, and a behaviour test is not a security scan.
A gate that cannot run in this repo is worse than no gate — it makes people believe they are protected. Do not install one.
When an upstream gate fails, skip the dependent gate and record that it was skipped and why; a skip is neither a pass nor an independent second failure.
A standard is a floor, not a template: complete headings over unclear content is still incomplete.
Removing a mechanism requires naming the defect class that would lose its owner, and the mechanism that takes over the path.
Confirm the available inputs cover the work before starting; if a critical input is missing, stop and say what is missing rather than filling the gap by assumption.

Unresolved items get classified: judgement calls go to the owner, factual questions get answered before the plan is executable. A plan that looks complete while carrying unverified assumptions is worse than no plan.
State inferred values before acting on them.
Acceptance thresholds come from the requester; only what the code already determines may be inferred.

Default to fewer, larger units of work. Split only at a context boundary, a human decision point, a failure-isolation boundary, or a deployment boundary; merge consecutive units that touch the same files with the same risk shape; and a two-or-three-file change is rarely its own unit.
Do not work directly on a protected branch, and do not run destructive git commands without explicit permission.
Commit messages must be scope-accurate against their diff and say why, not only what.
AI-generated changes reach a protected branch through human review.
Do not invent a parallel log or record path when one already exists.
A framework, tooling or infrastructure failure encountered during the work gets recorded with its root cause and durable evidence, not worked around in silence.
Reviewer invocations are all written before any completion is accepted, so results cannot be cherry-picked after the fact.
A set derived from several sources is an additive union; an incomplete caller list cannot subtract what another branch declared.
